description: We are a team of high school students interested in space exploration, technology, coding, and design. For the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, we aim to create an interactive educational experience that simulates decision-making during a Moon or Mars mission. We combine creativity, science, and technology to make space exploration engaging and accessible for young people.
summary:
Lunar Shift is an educational decision game where the player is responsible for a small lunar base.

The player manages four systems: life support, power, food production and radiation protection. Each system starts with a limited amount of resources. During the game, seven different situations appear. The player has to choose between two possible actions in each situation.

There is not always one perfect answer. For example, protecting the crew from radiation can require more power. Repairing a life-support system can also use electricity, but delaying the repair can create a bigger problem later. This makes the player think about how different systems are connected.

We used NASA resources about environmental control and life-support systems, space radiation and lunar power systems while designing the situations in the game. We simplified the scientific information so that students our age could understand it more easily.

Our main goal is to teach students that a Moon mission depends on many connected systems and limited resources. We wanted to turn these ideas into a simple game instead of only explaining them through text.
details:
Lunar Shift is an educational decision game where the player manages a small Moon base. The aim of the game is to keep four important systems working: life support, power, food production and radiation protection.

During the game, the player faces seven different situations. These include a solar particle warning, an oxygen generation problem, a greenhouse failure, a power shortage and a water recovery problem. In every situation, the player has two choices. Each choice has both positive and negative effects, so the player has to think about which resource is more important at that moment.

For example, moving the crew to a protected shelter can increase radiation safety but use more power. Repairing the life support system can also use energy, but delaying the repair can create a bigger problem later.

We used NASA resources about life support systems, space radiation and lunar power systems while creating the game. We simplified the scientific information so that students can understand the main ideas more easily.

Our goal is to show that living and working on the Moon requires planning, problem solving and balancing limited resources. We wanted to explain these ideas through an interactive game instead of only using text or a presentation.
